categories.name: Focus & Discipline
categories.overview: Short practices for protecting attention, starting deliberately, and returning after disruption.

topics.name: Attention & Environment
topics.overview: Make the chosen task easier to notice and distractions harder to reach.

topics.name: Starting & Momentum
topics.overview: Reduce the distance between an intention and the first visible action.

topics.name: Consistency & Recovery
topics.overview: Build a repeatable return after missed plans, interruptions, and low-energy days.

contentUnits.title: Give attention one door
contentUnits.summary: Name one target before work begins so every open option does not compete at once.

blocks.content: One visible target
Before a focus block, write the single result you want to move. A clear target gives attention a place to return when another option appears.

interactions.prompt: Pause and name the one result that deserves your next focus block.

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Attention
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Protect the first minute
contentUnits.summary: The first action can either settle attention or invite another round of switching.

blocks.content: You sit down to draft a proposal. Messages are visible, and the document is blank. Your first minute should reduce choice, not add more input.
A useful opening move is both relevant and immediately doable.

interactions.prompt: Which first move best protects attention?
options: Silence alerts and write the proposal heading
Search for a better writing app
interactions.expectedResponse: Silence alerts and write the proposal heading

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Attention
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Name the attention leak
contentUnits.summary: A specific trigger is easier to redesign than a vague complaint about poor focus.

blocks.content: Instead of saying “I get distracted,” describe the moment: what you were doing, what appeared, and what you did next.
Precise observation turns self-criticism into a design problem.

interactions.prompt: What specific cue most often pulls you away from focused work?

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Attention
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Add one friction step
contentUnits.summary: A tiny obstacle can interrupt an automatic distraction long enough for a deliberate choice.

blocks.content: Move the tempting app off the first screen, sign out after use, or place the phone beyond arm’s reach during one focus block.
Choose one reversible change. The goal is a pause, not a perfect environment.

interactions.prompt: What one friction step will you add before your next focus block?

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Attention
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Measure the start delay
contentUnits.summary: Track the gap between the planned start and the first visible action without judging it.

blocks.content: For one task, note when you intended to begin and when the first real action happened. Measurement reveals where a plan needs support.
The number is information, not a score of your character.

interactions.prompt: Record the start delay in minutes for one task today.

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Starting
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Recall the entry step
contentUnits.summary: A task becomes easier to start when its first physical action is already defined.

blocks.content: “Work on the report” still contains many decisions. “Open the draft and write one heading” gives the body an entry point.
The entry step should be visible, specific, and possible in about two minutes.

interactions.prompt: Without rereading, name the three qualities of a useful entry step.

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Starting
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Shrink the opening move
contentUnits.summary: Discipline often begins by making the first commitment smaller than the resistance around it.

blocks.content: Start, then decide again
Commit to one tiny opening move instead of the whole task. Once movement exists, you can choose whether to continue with better information.

interactions.prompt: Choose a task and silently reduce it to one two-minute opening move.

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Starting
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Choose an if-then plan
contentUnits.summary: Connect a recognizable cue to a concrete first action instead of relying on a vague intention.

blocks.content: An if-then plan removes a decision from the moment of action: when the cue appears, the prepared opening move begins.
Useful plans name both the cue and the behavior.

interactions.prompt: Which option is a complete if-then plan?
options: I will finish everything before lunch
If I sit down at 9:00, I will open the draft and write one heading
interactions.expectedResponse: If I sit down at 9:00, I will open the draft and write one heading

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Starting
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Define the low-energy version
contentUnits.summary: A smaller version keeps the path visible when the ideal routine is unrealistic.

blocks.content: Your full routine may not fit every day. Decide in advance what still counts when time or energy is limited.
The minimum should preserve identity and direction without pretending to equal the full practice.

interactions.prompt: What is the honest low-energy version of one routine you value?

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Consistency
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Use the next-slot rule
contentUnits.summary: After a miss, replace an abstract promise with the next concrete opportunity to return.

blocks.content: When a planned session is missed, choose the next realistic time and opening move. Recovery becomes a scheduled behavior, not a mood.
Do not redesign the whole system while disappointed. Secure the next return first.

interactions.prompt: Write the next realistic time and first action for a routine you recently missed.

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Consistency
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Count your returns
contentUnits.summary: Recovery is a trainable behavior, so record returns instead of demanding a flawless streak.

blocks.content: A broken streak hides an important success: beginning again. Count each deliberate return after an interruption or missed day.
The measure rewards recovery without pretending interruptions do not matter.

interactions.prompt: How many deliberate returns have you made this week?

source.title: Evolve Focus & Discipline Editorial Guide — Consistency
source.creator: Evolve Editorial

contentUnits.title: Recall the recovery loop
contentUnits.summary: A simple sequence turns disruption into a practiced return rather than a verdict on discipline.

blocks.content: Recovery has four moves: notice the break, reset one condition, take the smallest useful action, and record the return.
The loop is complete when action resumes, not when guilt feels resolved.

interactions.prompt: Without looking back, reconstruct the four moves of the recovery loop.
